interactions.label: Why has the incidence of multiple pregnancies increased globally in recent decad

params.question: Why has the incidence of multiple pregnancies increased globally in recent decades?

answers.text: Improved maternal nutrition leading to higher ovulation rates

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Maternal nutrition affects fertility broadly but is not the cause of the global rise in twins. The video explains that assisted reproductive technology — ovulation induction and IVF with multiple embryo transfer — is the principal driver.

answers.text: Widespread use of assisted reproductive technology, including ovulation induction and IVF

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. ART drives the rise: clomiphene-induced ovulation carries a 6–8% twin rate, and IVF with double embryo transfer historically produced twins in 25–30% of cycles. Single-embryo-transfer policies are reducing this, but ART-related multiples remain common.

answers.text: Higher rates of consanguineous marriages promoting dizygotic twinning

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Consanguinity does not increase dizygotic twinning. Dizygotic twins arise from two separate oocytes, which is influenced by maternal FSH levels, family history, and ART — not consanguinity.

answers.text: Increasing use of progesterone supplementation in early pregnancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Progesterone supplementation supports an existing implantation but does not increase the number of embryos. The established cause of rising multiple pregnancy rates is the widespread use of ART.

overallFeedback.feedback: The video explains that the main driver is widespread use of assisted reproductive technology: clomiphene carries a 6–8% twin rate, and IVF with double embryo transfer produces twins 25–30% of the time.
Well done. ART — especially ovulation induction and multi-embryo IVF transfer — is the main reason multiple pregnancies are increasing worldwide.

params.question: What does the lambda (twin peak) sign on first-trimester ultrasound indicate about a twin pregnancy?

answers.text: The twins share a single placenta with high risk of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The lambda sign indicates the opposite — separate placentas. A shared placenta is identified by the T-sign, where the inter-twin membrane meets the placental surface at a sharp right angle.

answers.text: The twins are monochorionic monoamniotic with no dividing membrane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In monoamniotic twins there is no inter-twin membrane at all. The lambda sign specifically shows a wedge of placental tissue extending into the base of a visible membrane, confirming two separate chorionic sacs.

answers.text: Each twin has its own placenta, with placental villi extending into the inter-twin membrane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The lambda sign shows a wedge of placental tissue from both placentas growing into the base of the inter-twin membrane. This is pathognomonic of dichorionic diamniotic twins — the lowest-risk twin configuration.

answers.text: Chorionicity cannot be determined and a repeat scan is needed after 14 weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The lambda sign is a definitive marker of dichorionic placentation. After 14 weeks the membrane thickens and chorionicity becomes harder to determine — which is precisely why the first-trimester scan (11–14 weeks) is the optimal window.

overallFeedback.feedback: The lambda (twin peak) sign shows a wedge of placental tissue extending into the inter-twin membrane, confirming that each twin has its own placenta (dichorionic diamniotic). It is best identified at 11–14 weeks.
Exactly right. The lambda sign confirms dichorionic placentation — the safest twin category — and is best identified at the 11–14 week scan before the membrane thickens.

params.question: A monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 22 weeks shows one twin with oligohydramnios and the other with polyhydramnios on ultrasound. Which complication is most likely responsible?

answers.text: Selective intrauterine growth restriction due to unequal placental territory

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Selective growth restriction causes discordant fetal size but does not produce the classic oligohydramnios–polyhydramnios pairing. That combination points to TTTS, where unbalanced blood flow through shared placental vessels depletes one twin and overloads the other.

answers.text: Premature rupture of membranes in the smaller twin's sac

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PPROM causes fluid loss from one sac, but the co-twin would not develop polyhydramnios. The combination of oligohydramnios in one twin AND polyhydramnios in the other is the hallmark of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome.

answers.text: Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome from unbalanced flow through shared placental vessels

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In TTTS, arteriovenous anastomoses in the shared monochorionic placenta cause unequal blood flow — the donor twin becomes volume-depleted (oligohydramnios) while the recipient becomes overloaded (polyhydramnios). Left untreated, the mortality risk is extremely high.

answers.text: Congenital renal agenesis in the smaller twin causing reduced urine output

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Renal agenesis can cause oligohydramnios in a singleton, but it does not explain polyhydramnios in the co-twin. The paired amniotic fluid discordance in a monochorionic pregnancy is the hallmark of TTTS.

overallFeedback.feedback: In a monochorionic twin pregnancy, oligohydramnios in one twin paired with polyhydramnios in the other is the hallmark of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome — unbalanced blood flow through shared placental vessels depletes the donor and overloads the recipient.
Correct. The oligohydramnios–polyhydramnios sequence in monochorionic twins is the classic presentation of TTTS, caused by unbalanced arteriovenous flow through shared placental vessels.

interactions.label: An uncomplicated dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy is progressing well at 36

params.question: An uncomplicated dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy is progressing well at 36 weeks. When should elective delivery be planned?

answers.text: Immediately at 36 weeks, since all twin pregnancies should deliver by this gestation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Delivery at 36–37 weeks is the recommendation for monochorionic diamniotic twins, who share one placenta and face TTTS risk. DCDA twins have separate placentas and a lower risk profile, so they can safely continue to 38 weeks.

answers.text: At 38 weeks, matching the lower risk associated with separate placentation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. DCDA twins carry the lowest risk among twin pregnancies because each has its own placenta. Planned delivery at 38 weeks balances the late stillbirth risk seen in all twins against fetal maturity.

answers.text: At 40 weeks, the same as for a singleton pregnancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Twin pregnancies should not continue to 40 weeks. Even DCDA twins have increased stillbirth risk beyond 38 weeks because of greater placental demands, so 38 weeks is the recommended delivery point.

answers.text: At 32 to 34 weeks by caesarean section, due to cord entanglement risk

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Delivery at 32–34 weeks is reserved for monochorionic monoamniotic twins, who share a single amniotic sac and face the highest risk of cord entanglement. DCDA twins have separate sacs and placentas, allowing safe continuation to 38 weeks.

overallFeedback.feedback: Delivery timing follows the chorionicity tree: DCDA at 38 weeks (lowest risk, separate placentas), MCDA at 36–37 weeks (shared placenta, TTTS risk), and MCMA at 32–34 weeks (shared sac, cord entanglement). DCDA twins safely continue to 38 weeks.

Well done. DCDA twins are the lowest-risk category — delivery at 38 weeks avoids late stillbirth risk while maximising fetal maturity. Remember the chorionicity tree: DCDA 38 weeks, MCDA 36–37 weeks, MCMA 32–34 weeks.
